alt: Particle diagrams: a solid has particles touching in a regular pattern, vibrating in place; a liquid has particles touching but random, sliding past each other; a gas has particles far apart, moving fast in all directions. Below each are its forces, shape, volume and how easily it compresses: only the gas compresses easily.
caption: Gases compress because their particles are far apart; solids and liquids are already touching.

alt: A glass tube has cotton wool soaked in ammonia at one end and hydrogen chloride at the other. Ammonia particles are lighter and move faster, so the white ring of ammonium chloride forms nearer the hydrogen chloride end. Diffusion is fastest in gases, faster at higher temperature and for lighter particles.
caption: The ring forms nearer the heavier gas, because lighter particles diffuse faster.

alt: A triangle of solid, liquid and gas. Melting, boiling or evaporation, and sublimation absorb energy; freezing, condensation and deposition release it. During any change of state the temperature stays constant because the energy overcomes forces between particles.
caption: Changes towards gas absorb energy; changes towards solid release it.

alt: A heating curve: temperature rises while the solid warms, stays flat for 120 s while it melts, rises while the liquid warms, then stays flat for 600 s while it boils. With a 100 W heater, melting takes 12 000 J and boiling 60 000 J, five times as much, because boiling separates the particles completely.
caption: Flat sections are changes of state; the longer boiling plateau shows boiling needs more energy.

alt: Left: a 6.0 × 3.0 × 2.0 cm block of mass 97.2 g has volume 36 cm³ and density 2.7 g/cm³ (2700 kg/m³), so it sinks in water. Right: an ornament of mass 112.5 g raises the water in a measuring cylinder from 50.0 to 62.5 cm³, a volume of 12.5 cm³ and a density of 9.0 g/cm³.
caption: Measure or displace to find the volume, then divide mass by volume.

alt: Four cases for a fixed amount of gas. Heating a sealed can makes particles faster, with more frequent, harder collisions, so pressure rises. Squashing a syringe gives more collisions per second, so pressure rises. Heating a balloon pushes its walls out, so volume increases. Cooling a balloon slows the particles, so it shrinks.
caption: Pressure comes from particles hitting the walls: change their speed or space and the pressure changes.

alt: Left: filtration through a filter funnel, with sand left as residue on the paper and water passing through as filtrate. Right: simple distillation of seawater. The flask is heated, a thermometer sits at the side arm, vapour passes through a water-cooled condenser with cold water in at the lower end, and pure water collects in a beaker while salt stays behind.
caption: Filtration removes insoluble solids; distillation recovers the solvent from a solution.

alt: A chromatogram with a pencil baseline above the solvent. The solvent front moved 9.0 cm; an ink separated into spots at 3.6 cm and 6.3 cm, giving Rf values of 0.40 and 0.70, so the ink contains at least two dyes. A reference spot level with the 6.3 cm spot would be the same substance.
caption: Rf = spot distance ÷ solvent distance, both from the baseline; a pure substance gives one spot.
